title: Natural and artificial immunity
log: 2026-11-01T14:46:35Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new
2026-11-01T14:55:56Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

match.reason: The bank point teaches herd immunity, a population-level effect of vaccination, while the new point teaches the difference between active immunity (your own antibodies) and passive immunity (received antibodies), so no bank point covers the same idea.

draft.title: Natural and artificial immunity
card: The body makes its own antibodies and memory cells after meeting an antigen. It takes days to start, but it can last for years.
The body receives antibodies made by another person or animal. It works straight away, but the antibodies break down, so protection fades. No memory cells form.
Immunity gained in everyday life. Catching an infection gives active immunity. Antibodies passed from mother to baby, across the placenta or in breast milk, give passive immunity.
Immunity gained through medical treatment. A vaccine gives active immunity. An injection of antibodies made elsewhere gives passive immunity.
draft.remember: Active: you make the antibodies and memory cells. Passive: you are given the antibodies.

a.q: Which person has gained active immunity?
opts: A child who made antibodies after a measles vaccine
A baby who received antibodies in breast milk
A patient given antibodies made by another person
A baby who received antibodies across the placenta
a.why: After a vaccine, the child's own B cells make antibodies and memory cells, so the immunity is active. In the other three cases the antibodies were made by someone else, so the immunity is passive. Breast milk is natural, but it is still passive.

b.q: Tom is bitten by a snake in Gippsland. He is given antibodies that were made in another animal. Which type of immunity does this give him?
b.why: Tom is given antibodies he did not make, so the immunity is passive. It comes from medical treatment, so it is artificial. Artificial active immunity is tempting, but it needs the body to make its own antibodies, as a vaccine does.
b.clue: Decide who made the antibodies, then whether it was medical treatment.

a.best: A child who made antibodies after a measles vaccine
